passage_title: Host Leaves, Temperature, and Tessan Beetle Larvae
passage:
Tessan beetles are leaf-eating insects found in upland meadows. Their larvae feed on the leaves of two local shrubs, Brell and Cormin. Entomologists studied how host plant, temperature, and a coating of fine silica powder on the leaves affected larval growth and survival.

In every trial, 20 newly hatched larvae were each placed alone in a covered dish and given fresh leaves daily for 14 days. On day 14, the entomologists recorded the percent of larvae still alive and the average mass of the surviving larvae. Table 1 gives the results.

Experiment 1
Larvae were fed Brell leaves or Cormin leaves at 22°C. No silica was applied.

Experiment 2
Larvae were fed Brell leaves at 16°C, 19°C, 25°C, or 28°C. No silica was applied. (The 22°C result for Brell is that of Experiment 1.)

Experiment 3
Brell leaves were dusted with silica powder at 2 or 6 grams per square meter (g/m²) of leaf surface before being fed to larvae at 22°C. (The 0 g/m² result is that of Experiment 1.)
prompt: Among the trials in which larvae were fed Brell leaves with no silica, the average larval mass was greatest at which temperature?
explanation: Brell, no silica: 18.4 mg (16°C), 31.0 mg (19°C), 41.6 mg (22°C), 44.2 mg (25°C), 36.5 mg (28°C). The greatest is 44.2 mg at "25°C".

subskill: locate a maximum within one series

passage_title: Glow Time of Lumivae Gel
passage:
Lumivae are single-celled algae that store energy from light and later release some of it as a faint green glow. A design team embedded Lumivae in a clear gel to make a coating that glows in the dark, and tested how long the coating glows.

In each trial, a 10 cm × 10 cm panel was coated with gel containing the same number of Lumivae per cubic centimeter. The panel was exposed to a lamp of fixed brightness for a set time and then moved into a dark chamber held at a set temperature. A light sensor recorded the glow duration: the time until the glow fell below a fixed detection level. Table 1 gives the results.

Experiment 1
Panels with gel 2 mm thick were exposed for 1, 2, 4, 8, or 16 minutes. The dark chamber was at 20°C.

Experiment 2
Panels with gel 1, 4, or 6 mm thick were exposed for 8 minutes. The dark chamber was at 20°C. (The 2 mm result is that of Experiment 1.)

Experiment 3
Panels with gel 2 mm thick were exposed for 8 minutes. The dark chamber was at 10°C or 30°C. (The 20°C result is that of Experiment 1.)
prompt: In Experiment 1, increasing the exposure time from 8 minutes to 16 minutes increased the glow duration by:
choices: 1 min.
4 min.
7 min.
11 min.
correct_answer: 1 min.
explanation: Glow duration was 22 min at 8 minutes and 23 min at 16 minutes, an increase of "1 min."
domain: Interpretation of Data
subskill: compute a difference between rows

consistency_check: Exposure-duration relation saturates (22 to 23 min from 8 to 16 min) rather than following any formula; thickness has an optimum at 4 mm; warmer chambers shorten the glow; the 8 min/2 mm/20°C trial is shared and listed once.

passage_title: Insect Visits to Merrow Flowers
passage:
Merrow is a meadow wildflower that comes in white, yellow, and violet forms. Ecologists planted Merrow in patches in an open meadow beside a forest and counted visits by pollinating insects.

In each trial, potted Merrow plants were set out in a square patch on a calm, sunny morning. Observers counted every insect landing on a flower for 2 hours and reported the number of visits per flower per hour. Each value in Table 1 is the average of 6 mornings.

Experiment 1
Patches of 5, 10, 20, or 40 white-flowered plants were placed 50 m from the forest edge.

Experiment 2
Patches of 20 yellow-flowered or 20 violet-flowered plants were placed 50 m from the forest edge. (The white result is that of Experiment 1.)

Experiment 3
Patches of 20 white-flowered plants were placed 10 m or 200 m from the forest edge. (The 50 m result is that of Experiment 1.)
prompt: In Experiment 1, the fewest visits per flower per hour were recorded in the patch with:
choices: 10 plants.
20 plants.
5 plants.
40 plants.
correct_answer: 5 plants.
explanation: Experiment 1 gave 3.1 (5 plants), 4.6 (10), 5.2 (20), and 4.0 (40). The fewest was in the patch with "5 plants."
domain: Interpretation of Data
subskill: locate a minimum within one series

consistency_check: Averages of 6 mornings, so one decimal place; patch size shows an optimum at 20 plants; yellow > white > violet at 50 m; visits fall with distance from the forest; the 20-white-50 m trial is shared and listed once.

passage_title: When Kessa Frogs Begin to Call
passage:
Kessa frogs live in a northern marsh. Each summer, males begin calling at night to attract females. In most years, calling begins between July 26 and August 1. At the marsh, day length is longest (about 16.1 hours) on June 21 and falls below 15.5 hours on about July 21. Midges, the frogs' main food, emerge from the water in large numbers on about July 20 in most years. Water temperature in the marsh first stays above 21°C for 10 nights in a row in late July in most years. Three scientists explain what starts the calling.

Scientist 1
Calling is triggered by warm water. Males begin calling as soon as the water has stayed above 21°C for 10 nights in a row. A single warm night, or a few warm nights, does not start calling. Day length and food do not affect when calling begins.

Scientist 2
Calling is triggered by shortening days. When day length falls below 15.5 hours, the males' bodies begin preparing to breed, and this preparation takes about 1 week. Calling therefore begins about 1 week after day length falls below 15.5 hours. Water temperature and food do not affect when calling begins.

Scientist 3
Calling is triggered by food. When the midges emerge, males feed heavily, and building up the energy reserves needed for calling takes about 1 week. Calling therefore begins about 1 week after the midges emerge, whatever the day length or water temperature.
prompt: In one year, the midges emerged on July 6, about two weeks earlier than usual. Day length and water temperature followed their usual pattern, and males began calling on July 28. This observation weakens the view of which scientist(s)?
choices: Scientist 3 only
Scientist 1 only
Scientist 2 only
Scientists 1 and 3 only
correct_answer: Scientist 3 only
explanation: Scientist 3 predicts calling about 1 week after the midges emerge, around July 13, not July 28. Scientists 1 and 2 predict late July in a year with usual water temperatures and day length, so "Scientist 3 only" is weakened.
domain: Evaluation of Models, Inferences, and Experimental Results
subskill: test viewpoints against a new finding
consistency_check: Day length at ~49 deg N recomputed from solar declination: ~16.1 h on June 21, ~15.5 h near July 21 (a 1 h drop takes until early August, so a 15 h trigger in mid-July would be impossible). passage_title: The Dark Bands of Tarrow Beach
passage:
At the back of Tarrow Beach, a low cliff of sand 1.2 m high has been cut by waves. The cliff shows 9 dark bands, each 1 to 4 cm thick, separated by thicker layers of light-colored sand. The dark bands are made mostly of dark mineral grains that are denser than the light grains. Mount Ell, a volcano, lies 60 km north of the beach, and winds there usually blow from the north. Two scientists explain how the dark bands formed.

Scientist 1
Each dark band formed during a single major storm. Large storm waves wash over the beach and throw sand far up onto the back of the beach. The waves carry light grains back to the sea more easily than the denser dark grains, so a layer rich in dark grains is left behind. The dark grains come from the beach's own sand; they have been rolled by waves for a long time, so they are rounded and match the dark sand now on the beach. Storms strong enough to reach the back of the beach strike about once every 10 years. Stronger storms move more sand, so they leave thicker dark bands.

Scientist 2
Each dark band formed from the ash of a single eruption of Mount Ell. Ash blown south by the wind settled on the beach and was buried by light sand. Ash grains are bits of volcanic glass, so they are sharp-edged, not rounded. Because the ash came from the north, each band should be thicker at the north end of the cliff than at the south end. Larger eruptions spread more ash, so they leave thicker dark bands. Written records list eruptions in 1912, 1951, and 1989, but smaller eruptions may not have been recorded.

choices: Scientist 2, because the dark grains match the dark sand now on the beach.
Scientist 1, because each dark band formed during a single storm.
Scientist 1, because the dark grains were worn round by waves on the beach itself.
Scientist 2, because the dark grains are rounded.
correct_answer: Scientist 1, because the dark grains were worn round by waves on the beach itself.
explanation: Scientist 1 says the dark grains are rounded and match the beach's own dark sand; Scientist 2 says they are sharp volcanic glass. So the finding supports "Scientist 1, because the dark grains were worn round by waves on the beach itself." Tamarel is an evergreen shrub planted along a busy road through a city park. Over the last three years, many of the park's Tamarel shrubs have developed yellow spots on their leaves. On a Tamarel shrub, the oldest leaves are the lowest ones, and new leaves grow at the tips of the branches. Three scientists explain the spots.

Scientist 1
The spots are caused by a fungus. Its spores live in the soil and are splashed onto leaves by raindrops, so spots appear first on the lowest leaves and spread upward over the summer. The fungus also spreads from shrub to shrub. Spraying a fungicide (a chemical that kills fungi) stops new spots from appearing.

Scientist 2
The spots are caused by a shortage of a trace mineral, which the scientists call T, in the park's soil. When T is scarce, a shrub moves T out of its oldest leaves into its new leaves, so spots appear first on the oldest leaves, which are the lowest ones. Adding fertilizer containing T to the soil stops new spots from appearing within 3 weeks. Spots do not spread from shrub to shrub.

Scientist 3
The spots are caused by ozone, a gas formed from vehicle exhaust in sunlight. Ozone is most concentrated within about 100 m of the road, so shrubs farther than 100 m from the road should have no spots. Spots appear on the upper surfaces of leaves, at any height on the shrub, and are worst after hot, sunny days.

choices: Scientist 1 only

correct_answer: Scientist 3 only
explanation: Scientist 3 says shrubs farther than 100 m from the road should have no spots. Scientists 1 and 2 say nothing about distance from the road, so "Scientist 3 only" is weakened.
